items.prompt: In graph theory, what are the two basic building blocks of any graph?
choices: Nodes (entities) and edges (relationships between pairs of nodes)
Rows and columns
Parents and children
Keys and values
items.explanation: A graph is nothing more than a set of nodes (also called vertices — the entities, like cities or services) and a set of edges connecting pairs of them (the relationships, like flight routes or service calls). Every other graph concept — directed, weighted, cyclic — is a property layered on top of that same two-part structure.
items.reference:
Graph = nodes + edges. SEA and MIA are nodes; the flight route between them is an edge.

Why: every other graph concept (directed, weighted, cyclic) is a property added on top of this two-part structure, not a replacement for it.

items.prompt: In a graph modeling a flight network, what does a node represent?
choices: A city (an airport)
A flight route between two cities
The price of a ticket
The airline operating a flight
items.explanation: The nodes are the entities being connected — in the flight network, that's the cities/airports themselves (SEA, DEN, ORD...). The routes between them are the edges, not the nodes.
items.reference:
Graph = nodes + edges. SEA and MIA are nodes; the flight route between them is an edge.

Why: every other graph concept (directed, weighted, cyclic) is a property added on top of this two-part structure, not a replacement for it.

items.prompt: In a graph modeling a flight network, what does an edge represent?
choices: A direct route between two cities
A city
The airline's headquarters
A passenger's itinerary across the whole trip
items.explanation: An edge is the relationship between exactly two nodes — a single direct flight leg, e.g. SEA to DEN. A full itinerary spanning multiple legs is a *path* through several edges, not a single edge itself.
items.reference:
Graph = nodes + edges. SEA and MIA are nodes; the flight route between them is an edge.

Why: every other graph concept (directed, weighted, cyclic) is a property added on top of this two-part structure, not a replacement for it.

items.prompt: A Facebook-style mutual friendship (if A is friends with B, B is automatically friends with A) is best modeled as which kind of graph?
choices: Undirected
Directed
Neither — friendships aren't graphs
Weighted only
items.explanation: Because the relationship holds equally in both directions, one edge between A and B represents the whole friendship — that's the definition of an undirected graph. A directed graph would need two separate edges (A→B and B→A) to express the same symmetric relationship, which is redundant here.
items.reference:
Directed: edge only goes one way (A follows B ≠ B follows A). Undirected: edge is symmetric (A friends B = B friends A).

Why: a directed flight route (SEA→DEN) doesn't imply the reverse fare exists — that's the tell for 'directed'.

items.prompt: A one-way Instagram 'follow' (you can follow someone who doesn't follow you back) is best modeled as which kind of graph?
choices: Directed
Undirected
Unweighted only, never directed
It can't be a graph at all
items.explanation: Because A following B doesn't imply B follows A, the relationship is asymmetric — exactly what a directed graph is for. A directed edge from A to B captures 'A follows B' without claiming anything about the reverse.
items.reference:
Directed: edge only goes one way (A follows B ≠ B follows A). Undirected: edge is symmetric (A friends B = B friends A).

Why: a directed flight route (SEA→DEN) doesn't imply the reverse fare exists — that's the tell for 'directed'.

items.prompt: A flight route SEA→DEN exists at $120, but there's no guarantee a DEN→SEA fare exists at the same price (or at all). What does this tell you about how to model the flight network?
choices: As a directed graph — each route is a one-way edge
As an undirected graph — routes are always symmetric
It means the network isn't a graph
It means every edge must be unweighted
items.explanation: A route existing in one direction doesn't guarantee the reverse route (or its price) — that asymmetry is exactly what a directed edge captures. Modeling it as undirected would silently assume a reverse fare exists whenever a forward one does, which the scenario itself contradicts.
items.reference:
Directed: edge only goes one way (A follows B ≠ B follows A). Undirected: edge is symmetric (A friends B = B friends A).

Why: a directed flight route (SEA→DEN) doesn't imply the reverse fare exists — that's the tell for 'directed'.

items.prompt: You only need to know whether a service *can* reach another service at all, not how many hops or how expensive the calls are. Should you model the graph as weighted or unweighted?
choices: Unweighted — every edge is treated as one equal step
Weighted — you always need weights, even if you don't use them
Neither — reachability isn't a graph question
It must be directed to be unweighted
items.explanation: If the only question is 'does a path exist,' assigning a cost to each edge adds bookkeeping you never use. An unweighted graph — where every edge counts the same — is both simpler and sufficient for pure reachability questions.
items.reference:
Weighted: every edge carries a cost/distance (flight price). Unweighted: every edge counts as exactly 1 step.

Why: the same flight network can be asked two different questions — fewest hops (unweighted view) or cheapest total (weighted view) — and the answers can differ.

items.prompt: The flight network's SEA→MIA question had two different 3-hop answers, $300 and $270. What made the difference between them visible in the first place?
choices: The graph is weighted — each edge carries its own dollar cost
The graph is directed
The graph has a cycle
The nodes have different degrees
items.explanation: Both routes tie at 3 hops, so an unweighted view (which only counts steps) can't distinguish them at all. The $30 gap only becomes visible once each edge carries its own weight (dollar cost) — that's precisely what 'weighted' means.
items.reference:
Weighted: every edge carries a cost/distance (flight price). Unweighted: every edge counts as exactly 1 step.

Why: the same flight network can be asked two different questions — fewest hops (unweighted view) or cheapest total (weighted view) — and the answers can differ.

items.prompt: Which of these is naturally modeled as a directed graph where an edge from a module to another means 'imports from'?
choices: A codebase's module/package dependency structure
A round-trip flight with a return ticket at the same price
A single node with no connections
A list of unrelated numbers
items.explanation: Module A importing module B doesn't mean B imports A back — that asymmetry is exactly what a directed edge captures, and it's why circular-import detection is a graph-cycle problem (the same kind of problem as L3's service dependency cycle).

items.prompt: A git commit history, where each commit points to its parent commit(s), is an example of which kind of graph?
choices: A directed graph (each edge points from a commit to its parent)
An undirected graph
Not a graph — it's a linear list only
A weighted graph where the weight is the commit message length
items.explanation: Each commit's parent pointer is a one-way edge (child → parent), and a merge commit can have more than one parent, which is exactly graph structure, not a plain list. Git history is one of the most common real-world directed graphs a working engineer touches daily.

items.prompt: In the flight network, MIA only appears as a destination (ATL→MIA), never as an origin for any listed route. In graph terms, what does that make MIA?
choices: A node with an out-degree of 0 (no outgoing edges) among the listed routes
Not a valid node at all
A node that must be removed from the graph
The start of every path
items.explanation: Degree just counts edges touching a node. 'Out-degree 0' means no edges point away from MIA in this data — it's still a perfectly valid node, just one with nothing further to reach from it (in this partial network).

items.prompt: SEA has two outgoing routes (to DEN and to ORD). What is SEA's out-degree?
choices: 5 — one per city in the whole network
items.explanation: Out-degree simply counts how many edges point away from a node. SEA has exactly two outgoing edges in the listed data (to DEN and to ORD), so its out-degree is 2 — regardless of how many total cities exist in the network.

items.prompt: ATL has incoming routes from both DEN and ORD, plus an outgoing route to MIA. What is ATL's in-degree?
items.explanation: In-degree counts edges pointing *into* a node. ATL receives edges from DEN and from ORD — two incoming edges — regardless of its separate outgoing edge to MIA, which counts toward out-degree instead.

items.prompt: A graph has 100 nodes and 300 edges. Roughly how many cells does an adjacency matrix need, versus an adjacency list?
choices: Matrix: 10,000 (100²). List: roughly 400 (100 nodes + 300 edges).
Matrix: 300. List: 10,000.
Both need exactly 10,000 regardless of representation.
Both need exactly 400 regardless of representation.
items.explanation: A matrix always costs V² cells — 100×100 = 10,000 — no matter how many real edges exist. A list costs roughly V + E — about 100 + 300 = 400 — because it only stores entries for edges that actually exist. This gap is exactly why sparse real-world graphs favor lists.
items.reference:
List: ~O(V+E) — one entry per node plus one per edge. Matrix: O(V²) — a full grid regardless of how sparse the graph is.

Why: real-world graphs (flight networks, service graphs) are almost always sparse, so the list wins in practice.

items.prompt: Why does a sparse graph (most pairs of nodes have no direct edge) favor an adjacency list over an adjacency matrix?
choices: The matrix's cost is fixed at V² regardless of sparsity, so most of its cells go unused; the list only stores edges that actually exist
Adjacency lists can only represent sparse graphs, never dense ones
Matrices are faster to build for any graph
Sparse graphs can't be represented as matrices at all
items.explanation: A matrix allocates a cell for every possible pair of nodes whether or not an edge exists there — in a sparse graph, most of that space is wasted. A list only pays for edges that are actually present, so its cost tracks the real edge count (E) instead of the worst case (V²).
items.reference:
List: ~O(V+E) — one entry per node plus one per edge. Matrix: O(V²) — a full grid regardless of how sparse the graph is.

Why: real-world graphs (flight networks, service graphs) are almost always sparse, so the list wins in practice.

items.prompt: When would an adjacency matrix actually be the better choice over a list?
choices: When the graph is dense (most pairs of nodes are connected) or 'is there an edge from A to B' needs to be an instant O(1) lookup
Whenever the graph has more than 10 nodes
Never — lists are strictly better in every case
Only for undirected graphs
items.explanation: A matrix's O(1) 'is A connected to B' lookup and its flat V² cost stop being a downside once the graph is dense enough that most cells would be filled anyway — at that point the list's per-edge savings shrink toward nothing, while the matrix keeps its fast direct-lookup advantage.
items.reference:
List: ~O(V+E) — one entry per node plus one per edge. Matrix: O(V²) — a full grid regardless of how sparse the graph is.

Why: real-world graphs (flight networks, service graphs) are almost always sparse, so the list wins in practice.

items.prompt: Traversing every edge in a graph (visiting each node and looking at its neighbors once) costs O(V + E) with an adjacency list. What does the same full traversal cost with an adjacency matrix, and why?
choices: O(V²) — checking every row for possible neighbors means scanning all V cells per node, for V nodes
O(V + E) — identical to the list
O(E) — the matrix skips empty cells automatically
O(1) — matrices are always instant to traverse
items.explanation: A matrix has no way to skip straight to a node's real neighbors — finding them means scanning that node's entire row (V cells) checking for non-empty entries, and there are V rows. A list, by contrast, only stores real edges, so walking every neighbor list touches exactly E entries total, giving O(V + E) instead of O(V²).
items.reference:
List: O(V+E) build/traversal. Matrix: O(V²) build/traversal, but O(1) direct edge lookup.

Why: the representation choice is a trade-off between total cost (favors list on sparse graphs) and single-lookup speed (favors matrix).

items.prompt: What is the trade-off being made when you choose an adjacency matrix over an adjacency list?
choices: You gain O(1) direct 'is there an edge from A to B' lookup, at the cost of O(V²) memory and build/traversal time regardless of how sparse the graph is
You gain faster traversal on every graph, with no downside
You gain less memory usage on sparse graphs
There is no trade-off — one representation strictly dominates the other
items.explanation: A matrix's fixed grid means checking whether a specific edge exists is a single cell lookup — O(1) — which a list can't match without scanning a neighbor list. That convenience costs O(V²) memory and build time no matter how few real edges exist, which is why the right choice depends on whether the graph is sparse (favor list) or dense with frequent single-edge lookups (favor matrix).
items.reference:
List: O(V+E) build/traversal. Matrix: O(V²) build/traversal, but O(1) direct edge lookup.

Why: the representation choice is a trade-off between total cost (favors list on sparse graphs) and single-lookup speed (favors matrix).

items.prompt: What data structure makes BFS explore a graph layer by layer instead of racing down one branch first?
choices: A FIFO queue (first in, first out)
A LIFO stack
A sorted array
A hash set with no ordering
items.explanation: A FIFO queue always processes the oldest-enqueued node next, which forces the search to finish an entire layer (all nodes at distance N) before moving to distance N+1. Swap the queue for a LIFO stack and the same traversal logic becomes depth-first search instead.
items.reference:
BFS: FIFO queue + visited set, explores layer by layer, finds fewest hops.

Why: queue order (not edge weight) is all BFS looks at — that's why it can return a valid-but-not-cheapest tie among equal-hop-count paths.

items.prompt: Why does BFS need a 'visited' set in addition to its queue?
choices: To avoid re-enqueuing a node it already reached by an equal-or-shorter path, which would waste work or loop forever on a cycle
To keep track of edge weights
To sort the nodes alphabetically before visiting
BFS doesn't actually need one — it's optional
items.explanation: Without tracking which nodes are already reached, BFS could re-enqueue the same node repeatedly — wasteful at best, and an infinite loop at worst if the graph has a cycle. The visited set also guarantees that the *first* time a node is dequeued, it's via the shortest possible hop count, since BFS explores strictly in layer order.
items.reference:
BFS: FIFO queue + visited set, explores layer by layer, finds fewest hops.

Why: queue order (not edge weight) is all BFS looks at — that's why it can return a valid-but-not-cheapest tie among equal-hop-count paths.

items.prompt: SEA→DEN→ATL→MIA ($300) and SEA→ORD→ATL→MIA ($270) are both 3 hops. Why might BFS report the more expensive one?
choices: BFS never inspects edge weight at all — which of two equal-hop-count paths it returns depends only on which neighbor happened to be enqueued first
BFS always returns the most expensive of several tied paths on purpose
This means BFS has a bug
BFS recalculates cost after finding the path and picks the worse one intentionally
items.explanation: BFS's entire notion of 'distance' is hop count, tracked purely through queue order — the algorithm's code never reads a weight field. Among multiple paths tied on hop count, whichever one's intermediate nodes got enqueued first is the one BFS reports, with no preference for cost.
items.reference:
BFS: FIFO queue + visited set, explores layer by layer, finds fewest hops.

Why: queue order (not edge weight) is all BFS looks at — that's why it can return a valid-but-not-cheapest tie among equal-hop-count paths.

items.prompt: What does it mean to 'relax an edge' in Dijkstra's algorithm?
choices: Checking whether going through the current node gives a neighbor a cheaper total cost than previously known, and updating it if so
Removing an edge from the graph permanently
Ignoring an edge's weight and treating it as 1
Doubling an edge's weight to be safe
items.explanation: Relaxing an edge is Dijkstra's core update step: for each neighbor of the node just expanded, compare 'cost so far to get here via this new route' against 'the best cost previously recorded for that neighbor,' and keep whichever is smaller. This is exactly how ATL's best-known cost dropped from $250 (via DEN) to $220 (via ORD) in the L2 trace.
items.reference:
Dijkstra: priority queue by lowest known cost + edge relaxation, guarantees cheapest total.

Why: unlike BFS, Dijkstra revisits a node's cost estimate whenever a cheaper route to it is found — that's the 'relax' step.

items.prompt: How does Dijkstra decide which unvisited node to expand next?
choices: Whichever unvisited node currently has the lowest known total cost from the start
Whichever node was added to the graph first
Whichever node has the most neighbors
A random unvisited node
items.explanation: Dijkstra always greedily expands the cheapest-so-far unvisited node next — this greedy choice is safe (guaranteed correct) specifically because edge weights are non-negative, so no undiscovered path could possibly beat the cheapest known option by going through a more expensive node first.
items.reference:
Dijkstra: priority queue by lowest known cost + edge relaxation, guarantees cheapest total.

Why: unlike BFS, Dijkstra revisits a node's cost estimate whenever a cheaper route to it is found — that's the 'relax' step.

items.prompt: You need the fewest number of retries before a request succeeds, and every retry costs the same regardless of which path it takes through a fallback chain. Which algorithm fits?
choices: BFS
Dijkstra
Neither — this isn't a graph problem
Both give wrong answers here
items.explanation: Since every 'step' (retry) costs the same, this is an unweighted-graph question — 'fewest hops' is exactly what BFS answers, and it's cheaper to run than Dijkstra for the same result here.
items.reference:
Unweighted / hop count → BFS. Weighted / total cost → Dijkstra.

Why: running BFS on a weighted graph when cost actually matters gives a plausible-looking wrong answer — the more dangerous failure of the two.

items.prompt: You need the cheapest total network egress cost across a chain of possible routes, where each hop has a different dollar cost per GB. Which algorithm fits?
choices: Dijkstra
BFS
Neither — this isn't a graph problem
Depth-first search, because it's faster
items.explanation: Costs vary per edge, so this is a weighted-graph question about total cost, not hop count — exactly what Dijkstra is built to answer. BFS would ignore the cost differences entirely and could return a cheap-looking-but-actually-expensive route.
items.reference:
Unweighted / hop count → BFS. Weighted / total cost → Dijkstra.

Why: running BFS on a weighted graph when cost actually matters gives a plausible-looking wrong answer — the more dangerous failure of the two.

items.prompt: Running BFS on a weighted graph where the weights genuinely matter (instead of running Dijkstra) is dangerous mainly because:
choices: It still returns a plausible-looking path, just not necessarily the cheapest one — the mistake doesn't announce itself
It always crashes with an error
It's slower than Dijkstra in every case
It can't handle directed graphs
items.explanation: BFS won't error out on a weighted graph — it'll happily return *a* valid path with the fewest hops, which looks like a reasonable answer. The bug is silent: nothing signals that cost was ignored, so a wrong-but-plausible route can ship unnoticed.
items.reference:
Unweighted / hop count → BFS. Weighted / total cost → Dijkstra.

Why: running BFS on a weighted graph when cost actually matters gives a plausible-looking wrong answer — the more dangerous failure of the two.

items.prompt: Implement buildAdjacencyList(edges), where edges is an array of [from, to] pairs. Return a plain object mapping each node name to an array of its outgoing neighbor names. Every node that appears anywhere in the edge list (as either 'from' or 'to') must be a key in the result, even if its neighbor list is empty.

tests.description: builds neighbor lists for a simple two-edge graph
a destination-only node still appears as a key with an empty list
an empty edge list returns an empty object

items.explanation: Every edge contributes a neighbor to its 'from' node's list, but both endpoints need to exist as keys first — otherwise a node that only ever appears as a destination (like MIA in a one-way flight network) would be missing from the object entirely, forcing every algorithm that walks this structure to handle a missing key as a special case instead of safely getting back an empty array.
items.reference:
buildAdjacencyList: for each edge, ensure both endpoints exist as keys, then push the edge onto the 'from' node's list.

Why: without the endpoint guard, a destination-only node (like MIA) would be missing from the map, forcing every downstream algorithm to special-case a missing key.

items.prompt: Implement buildWeightedAdjacencyList(edges), where edges is an array of [from, to, weight] triples. Return a plain object mapping each node to an array of {to, weight} objects. Every node appearing anywhere in the edge list must be a key, even with an empty array.

tests.description: builds a weighted neighbor list for a single edge
handles multiple outgoing edges from the same node
a destination-only node still gets an empty array key

items.explanation: This is the same shape as the unweighted version, just carrying the weight along in each neighbor entry instead of a bare name. Keeping the weight attached to the edge (rather than in a separate lookup) is what lets Dijkstra read edge.weight directly while walking the same structure BFS uses.
items.reference:
buildAdjacencyList: for each edge, ensure both endpoints exist as keys, then push the edge onto the 'from' node's list.

Why: without the endpoint guard, a destination-only node (like MIA) would be missing from the map, forcing every downstream algorithm to special-case a missing key.

items.prompt: Implement bfsShortestPath(adj, start, end), where adj is a plain object mapping each node to an array of neighbor names (unweighted). Return an array of node names forming the fewest-hops path from start to end, or null if end is unreachable.

tests.description: finds the direct path when start equals end
finds a 3-hop path through a branching graph
returns null when the end node is unreachable

items.explanation: queue.shift() pulls the oldest-enqueued node first, which is what keeps the search moving layer by layer (breadth-first) instead of racing down one branch. The cameFrom map records, for every newly-visited node, which node discovered it — walking that chain backwards from `end` and reversing it reconstructs the actual path, not just its length.
items.reference:
bfsShortestPath: FIFO queue + visited set + cameFrom pointers, rebuild the path by walking cameFrom backwards from the end.

Why: queue.shift() (not .pop()) is what keeps the search breadth-first — that's the one line the whole guarantee rests on.

items.prompt: Implement bfsShortestPath(adj, start, end) as above (plain object adjacency list, array of neighbor names). This variant's graph has two different routes tied on hop count — make sure your function returns a real 3-hop path, not just any array.

tests.description: the returned path starts at the start node
the returned path ends at the end node
the path has exactly 4 nodes (3 hops)

items.explanation: Both SEA→DEN→ATL→MIA and SEA→ORD→ATL→MIA are 3 hops, so either is a valid answer to 'fewest hops' — BFS's visited set ensures ATL is only ever reached once, via whichever of DEN/ORD got dequeued first. Which specific one 'wins' isn't guaranteed, but the hop count (4 nodes, 3 edges) always is.
items.reference:
bfsShortestPath: FIFO queue + visited set + cameFrom pointers, rebuild the path by walking cameFrom backwards from the end.

Why: queue.shift() (not .pop()) is what keeps the search breadth-first — that's the one line the whole guarantee rests on.

items.prompt: Implement bfsShortestPath(adj, start, end) as above. This variant tests the unreachable case specifically: start and end exist in the graph, but no path connects them.

tests.description: returns null for two nodes in disconnected components
still finds a path when one does exist
returns null for a node with no outgoing edges trying to reach anything else

items.explanation: When the queue empties out without ever dequeuing `end`, every node reachable from `start` has already been visited and none of them was the target — that's exactly what 'unreachable' means, and the loop falling through to `return null` after the while-loop is what reports it correctly.
items.reference:
bfsShortestPath: FIFO queue + visited set + cameFrom pointers, rebuild the path by walking cameFrom backwards from the end.

Why: queue.shift() (not .pop()) is what keeps the search breadth-first — that's the one line the whole guarantee rests on.

items.prompt: Implement dijkstraShortestPath(adj, start, end), where adj maps each node to an array of {to, weight} objects. Return {path, cost} for the cheapest total-weight path from start to end, or null if unreachable. The graph below has two 3-hop routes to MIA that differ in cost — make sure you return the cheaper one.

tests.description: finds the cheaper of two tied-hop-count routes
tests.expr: const g = {SEA:[{to:"DEN",weight:120},{to:"ORD",weight:150}], DEN:[{to:"ATL",weight:130}], ORD:[{to:"ATL",weight:70}], ATL:[{to:"MIA",weight:50}], MIA:[]}; expect(dijkstraShortestPath(g, "SEA", "MIA").cost).toBe(270)

tests.description: the cheaper path is returned, not the pricier tied-hop-count one
tests.expr: const g = {SEA:[{to:"DEN",weight:120},{to:"ORD",weight:150}], DEN:[{to:"ATL",weight:130}], ORD:[{to:"ATL",weight:70}], ATL:[{to:"MIA",weight:50}], MIA:[]}; expect(dijkstraShortestPath(g, "SEA", "MIA").path).toEqual(["SEA","ORD","ATL","MIA"])

tests.description: a direct single-edge path has cost equal to that edge's weight

items.explanation: Greedily expanding the cheapest known unvisited node each time is safe because weights are non-negative — no undiscovered route could beat the current best by first passing through something more expensive. The relax step (updating costSoFar and cameFrom whenever a cheaper route is found) is what lets ATL's recorded cost drop from $250 (via DEN) to $220 (via ORD) partway through the run, which is exactly why the final answer is the $270 route, not the $300 one.
items.reference:
dijkstraShortestPath: always expand the lowest-known-cost unvisited node next; relax each outgoing edge (update cost + cameFrom if a cheaper route is found).

Why: the relax step is what lets a later-discovered cheaper route overwrite an earlier, more expensive one for the same node.

items.prompt: Implement dijkstraShortestPath(adj, start, end) as above. This variant tests the unreachable case: end exists as a key in adj, but no path connects start to it.

tests.description: returns null when end is unreachable from start
tests.expr: const g = {A:[{to:"B",weight:5}], B:[], C:[{to:"D",weight:1}], D:[]}; expect(dijkstraShortestPath(g, "A", "C")).toBe(null)

tests.description: still finds the correct cost when a path does exist
start equal to end has cost 0

items.explanation: Once every node with a finite known cost has been visited and `end` was never among them, costSoFar never gains an entry for `end` — checking `costSoFar.has(end)` after the loop is what correctly reports unreachability instead of returning a bogus Infinity-cost path.
items.reference:
dijkstraShortestPath: always expand the lowest-known-cost unvisited node next; relax each outgoing edge (update cost + cameFrom if a cheaper route is found).

Why: the relax step is what lets a later-discovered cheaper route overwrite an earlier, more expensive one for the same node.

items.prompt: Implement hasCycle(adj), where adj maps each node to an array of neighbor names (a directed graph). Return true if the graph contains a cycle, false otherwise. Use the three-color DFS approach: white (unvisited), gray (on the current DFS path), black (fully explored) — reaching a gray node means a cycle.

tests.description: detects the checkout/inventory/pricing dependency cycle
the flight network (a DAG) has no cycle, even though ATL is reached from two directions
a graph with no edges at all has no cycle

items.explanation: The three colors distinguish 'still an ancestor on the current path' (gray) from 'fully explored and proven safe' (black) — a plain visited flag can't tell those apart. Reaching a gray node means the current DFS path has looped back on itself, which is a cycle; reaching a black node just means that subtree was already checked via a different, unrelated branch, which is exactly what happens when both DEN and ORD reach ATL in the acyclic flight network.
items.reference:
hasCycle: DFS with three colors — white (unvisited), gray (on the current path), black (fully explored). Reaching a gray node means a cycle.

Why: a plain visited/unvisited flag can't distinguish 'still open on this path' from 'already proven safe via another branch' — the flight graph's converging-but-acyclic paths through ATL prove why that distinction matters.

items.prompt: Implement hasCycle(adj) as above (directed graph, neighbor-name arrays). This variant's graph is a longer chain with a cycle further from the start node — make sure your DFS actually explores from every unvisited node, not just the first one.

tests.description: finds a cycle that isn't reachable from the first key in the object
a simple chain with no back edges has no cycle
a self-loop (a node pointing to itself) counts as a cycle

items.explanation: A single DFS from one starting node can only find cycles reachable from it — the outer loop that tries `visit` from every still-white node is what guarantees a cycle anywhere in the graph gets found, even in an unrelated component. A self-loop is the smallest possible cycle: the node is marked gray, then its own neighbor list immediately points back at that same gray node.
items.reference:
hasCycle: DFS with three colors — white (unvisited), gray (on the current path), black (fully explored). Reaching a gray node means a cycle.

Why: a plain visited/unvisited flag can't distinguish 'still open on this path' from 'already proven safe via another branch' — the flight graph's converging-but-acyclic paths through ATL prove why that distinction matters.

items.prompt: The array-scan version of Dijkstra shown in this unit picks the next node to expand by looping over every unvisited node. What is that pick step's complexity, and how does swapping in a binary min-heap change it?
choices: O(V) per pick with the array scan; O(log V) per pick with a heap
O(1) per pick either way — the data structure doesn't matter

items.prompt: bfsShortestPath and dijkstraShortestPath both need to handle the case where `end` is simply unreachable from `start`. What's the correct behavior, and what would go wrong without it?
